prime.problem: Batching fixes linear layers: share the weights and intensity climbs to B<sub>crit</sub>. Try the same on attention and nothing improves. If you don't know why, you'll spend effort on faster attention math that sits idle 99% of the time in decode.
prime.fits: Fifth card. It applies the roofline to the other kind of operation from the what we optimize split, right after linear layers, and derives why the KV term of the step-time formula is always memory-bound.
expect: KV bytes vs weight bytes per step
prime.goal: Derive attention's intensity, explain why B and D cancel, compute it for prefill, decode and GQA, and say which lever speeds up decode attention.

attend: In the Flash Attention accounting, which tensors are read from HBM, and which big tensor is never written?
Why do B and D cancel out of ST/(S+T), and what does that cancellation mean for batching?
What plays the role of reuse in prefill attention, and why does decode have none?
How does GQA change the bytes but not the FLOPs, and why does that push intensity toward G?
At what batch and context do KV bytes overtake weight bytes in a decode step, and why does that moment matter?

must: Flash Attention reads Q (2BTD) and K, V (4BSD), writes the output (2BTD) and does 4BSTD FLOPs → intensity = ST/(S+T) → B and D cancel, so neither batching nor a wider model raises it
Prefill has S = T → intensity T/2 → compute-bound past ≈ 480 tokens (v5e) or ≈ 590 (H100); decode has T = 1 → intensity S/(S+1) < 1 → memory-bound at every context and every batch

Each sequence brings its own KV cache → a second sequence adds as many bytes as FLOPs → unlike weights, nothing is shared → the attention term grows linearly in B × context and dominates a long-context step

GQA lets G query heads share each K/V row → bytes drop by G while FLOPs don't → decode intensity rises to ≈ G (4 for Llama-3.1-8B, 32 for MQA) → still far below 295, so the lever is fewer KV bytes, not faster math
elevated: KV bytes equal weight bytes when B · S<sub>KV</sub> = S<sub>params</sub> → 15 sequences at 8k for Llama-3.1-8B → the book's rule of thumb 2DF/(SHK) ≈ F vs S predicts when batching's gains start to fade
reference: the softmax FLOPs the book ignores
the book's Part 4 answer of compute-bound at S = 240 vs Part 7's 480
the GQA prefill crossover formula ridge · (G+1)/G

compress.prompt: From memory, write attention's FLOPs and bytes, simplify to ST/(S+T), and evaluate it for prefill (T = S = 4096) and decode (T = 1, S = 8192). Add the GQA version in one line. Then say in one sentence what that implies for the step-time formula's KV term.
checklist: FLOPs 4BSTD; bytes 4BSD + 4BTD; B and D cancel
so the KV term is just KV bytes ÷ bandwidth, never a FLOPs term

retrieve.q: Explain the book's point, conceptually, of why adding sequences raises a linear layer's intensity but not attention's.
answer: a linear layer's weights are the same for every sequence, so one load serves the whole batch
attention's K and V are different for every sequence, so each new sequence brings its own bytes
FLOPs and bytes grow together, so the ratio is stuck

retrieve.q: Walk through one decode step of attention for one sequence at S = 8,192 with the card's MHA-sized layer: what is read, how many FLOPs, what intensity?
answer: read the one new query (8 KB) and the whole K, V cache for that layer (134.2 MB)
one query meets every key: 4·S·T·D = 1.34e8 FLOPs

retrieve.q: A team proposes a faster attention kernel to cut decode latency at batch 64 and 8k context on Llama-3.1-8B. Using the card's whole-model check, how much can math improvements save, and what would you do instead?
answer: attention there is 2.75e11 FLOPs over 68.75 GB: 4.0 FLOPs/byte
T<sub>math</sub> = 0.28 ms vs T<sub>comms</sub> = 20.5 ms: arithmetic is idle ~99%
a faster matmul saves almost nothing; read fewer KV bytes (FP8 KV, GQA/MQA, paging that skips padding)

compare.q: Flash Attention is assumed inside ST/(S+T). What does it change about attention's bytes, why does that let prefill reach T/2, and why doesn't it rescue decode?
answer: it never writes the [B, S, T] score matrix to HBM, so bytes are just Q, K, V and the output
without that, the S·T scores would add bytes and cap prefill intensity well below T/2
decode still has to read the whole K, V cache for a single query row, so intensity stays ≈ 1 either way

compare.q: perf-1 introduced GQA as a way to shrink the KV cache. This card says it also raises intensity. Are those the same effect, and why is neither enough to make decode attention compute-bound?
answer: same cause: G query heads read one K/V row, so KV bytes drop by G for the same FLOPs
that shrinks the cache (4× for Llama-3.1-8B) and raises intensity from ≈ 1 to ≈ G
G is 4–32 in practice, far below a ridge of 240–295

predict.q: Llama-3.1-8B, one H100, batch 32 at 4k context. Commit first: how many GB of KV does one decode step read across all layers, how long does that take, and is the attention math more or less than 0.1 ms?
predict.answer: 32 × 4,096 × 131,072 B = 17.18 GB, which takes 17.18 / 3.35 TB/s = 5.13 ms. The math is 4 × B × S × N × H × L = 6.87e10 FLOPs = 0.069 ms at 989 TFLOPS: less than 0.1 ms. Intensity = 6.87e10 / 17.18e9 = 4.0 = G, exactly as the GQA formula predicts.

apply.task: Run labs/attention-intensity.py and add a row for Llama-3.1-8B decode at batch 32, S = 4,096: KV bytes, FLOPs, intensity, Tmath and Tcomms on an H100. Then compute the prefill crossover (the T at which prefill attention turns compute-bound) for a hypothetical G = 8 model on H100 and on v5e.
apply.done: Your decode row shows ≈ 17.2 GB, ≈ 6.9e10 FLOPs, intensity ≈ 4.0, T<sub>comms</sub> ≈ 5.13 ms against T<sub>math</sub> ≈ 0.07 ms, and your G = 8 crossovers are ≈ 332 tokens (H100) and 270 (v5e).
apply.hint: Crossover T = ridge × (G + 1)/G: 295 × 9/8 and 240 × 9/8. For decode, KV bytes = B × S × 131,072 and FLOPs = 4·B·S·N·H·L with N = 32, H = 128, L = 32.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the KV bytes, or how small the math is?
Could you explain why B cancels, in one sentence and without the formula?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: shared weights → intensity ≈ B, or private KV → intensity ≈ 1?
Can you say when the weights, not KV, still dominate a decode step?
What will you check on the step-time card: how this becomes its always-memory-bound first term?
